name: Personal Pronouns: Formal "De" vs. Informal "du"
explanation: "du" is the everyday, informal way to say "you", used with friends, family, and people you know well. In formal or professional writing — emails to clients, official contacts, or people you don't know — Danish traditionally uses the capitalized pronoun "De" (object form "Dem", possessive "Deres") instead. Modern Danish business culture leans increasingly informal, but "De" still signals politeness and distance in written correspondence.

examples.danish: Kunne De bekræfte mødet i morgen?
examples.english: Could you (formal) confirm the meeting tomorrow?
I am sending you (formal) the agenda attached.

name: Modal Phrases for Politeness (vil gerne, kunne, må jeg)
explanation: Modal verbs like "vil", "kunne" and "må" soften a request so it sounds polite rather than blunt — especially important in professional emails and meeting proposals. "Jeg vil gerne..." (I would like to...) and "Kunne De/vi...?" (Could you/we...?) are the standard polite openers in Danish business communication.

examples.danish: Jeg vil gerne booke et møde med Dem.
examples.english: I would like to book a meeting with you.

examples.danish: Kunne vi flytte mødet til fredag?
examples.english: Could we reschedule the meeting to Friday?

name: Inversion in Formal Written Openings
explanation: Danish main clauses always keep the verb in second position (the verb-second rule). Formal emails often open with something other than the subject — "Hermed", "Vedrørende...", a date or time — which pushes the subject after the verb. Recognizing and producing this word order is a key feature of professional written Danish.

examples.danish: Hermed bekræfter jeg vores møde på tirsdag.
examples.english: Hereby I confirm our meeting on Tuesday.

examples.danish: Vedrørende dagsordenen har jeg et par kommentarer.
examples.english: Regarding the agenda, I have a few comments.
